title: Attaching Biological Probes to Silica Optical Biosensors Using Silane Coupling Agents
protocol: Clean the surface of the devices using oxygen plasma or piranha solution.
Populate the cleaned surface with hydroxyl groups.
Expose the hydroxyl groups to vapor deposition of a silane coupling agent terminated with a primary amine.
Attach biotin to the surface via N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) ester chemistry.
Evaluate the surface functionalization protocols and potential contamination through optical microscopy after adding the primary amine.
Use fluorescence microscopy to verify the quality and uniformity of surface coverage of the biotin molecule.
Label the biotin groups on the surface using Texas Red fluorescent dye conjugated to avidin to confirm binding capability.
React fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) with primary amines to form stable, covalent thiourea linkage to the microsphere for amine coverage evaluation.
Use silane coupling agent as a bridge between the inorganic surface and organic probe molecule during functionalization.
Build the storage housing for the microspheres.
Cut a ¼ inch thick piece of cardboard into a 1 inch x 1 inch square.
Tape the cardboard square onto a regular-sized glass slide.
Attach a 1 inch section of scotch tape, with its ends meeting to form a roll, to the cardboard.
Cut a 3 inch section of optical fiber from a spool of optical fiber.
Strip the protective polymeric coating from the last 0.5 inches of the end of the cut piece of fiber using a No-Nik fiber-stripper.
Clean the surface of any remaining polymer with a Kimwipe dampened with methanol by gently wiping the fiber.
Trim the stripped end so that only about 1 millimeter of stripped fiber remains on the end of the fiber.
Place the stripped end of the optical fiber into the path of a CO2 laser.
Vertically align the fiber such that its stripped end is facing down.
Turn on the CO2 laser and direct it to the surface of the stripped end of the optical fiber.
Melt the stripped end of the fiber into a sphere using approximately 3.5% power in 2 seconds.
Carefully grasp the stem (the non-stripped portion of the optical fiber) of the microsphere with tweezers.
Attach the stem to the tape roll on the microsphere housing.
Store the glass slide containing the microsphere in a petri dish for safe storage.
Prepare a piranha solution by adding 5 ml of hydrogen peroxide and 11.6 mL of fuming sulfuric acid to a polypropylene vial.
Transfer the glass slide holding at least one microsphere into the piranha solution, ensuring the microsphere is in contact with the liquid but not touching the cardboard.
Gently remove the glass slide from the piranha solution and insert it into another plastic vial containing DDI H2O.
Let the samples sit in the DDI H2O for 5 minutes.
Gently remove the glass slide from the DDI H2O and place it in an oven at 80 °C to dry the surface for 10 minutes.
Transfer the glass slide containing at least one microsphere to the oxygen plasma chamber.
Set the oxygen pressure to 200 mTorr and the power to 120 W.
Expose the sample to the oxygen plasma for 2 minutes.
Remove the glass slide from the plasma chamber.
Place the glass slide, containing at least one microsphere, into a vacuum desiccator in a fume hood.
Open the silane coupling agent bottle and place it in the desiccator.
Replace the lid on the vacuum desiccator and attach the outlet port to an aspirator or house vacuum line.
Turn on the house vacuum or water line to evacuate the vacuum desiccator.
Begin timing the reaction once a vacuum seal is formed between the lid and the base.
After 15 minutes, turn off the vacuum.
Slowly open the port to let air into the desiccator.
Prepare a 10 mM solution of NHS-biotin in anhydrous DMSO.
Sonicate the NHS-biotin solution for 1 hour to fully dissolve the powder.
Transfer the glass slide containing microspheres into another plastic vial, with stems at the top and microspheres at the bottom.
Add an appropriate volume of NHS-biotin solution down the side of the vial, behind the glass slide, ensuring it covers the microsphere surface.
Incubate the vials on a rocking incubator at room temperature for 30 minutes at 5 rpm and 5 degrees tilt angle.
Gently remove the glass slide from the vial and transfer it into another vial filled with DDI H2O.
Place the vial containing the microsphere in DDI H2O on the tilt tray for 10 minutes at 5 rpm and 5 degrees tilt angle.
Repeat the water rinsing step twice more, each time using fresh DDI H2O.
Remove the glass slide from the vial.
Place the glass slide in an oven at 80 °C for 10 minutes.
Dissolve 1 mg FITC in 1 mL anhydrous DMSO in a darkened room.
Dilute the FITC solution by adding 50 μL to 1 mL of 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate buffer.
Place amine-terminated microspheres housed on the glass slide into a vial containing the diluted FITC solution.
Let the sample react with the FITC solution for a minimum of 4 hours in the dark.
Remove excess fluorophore through two, 10 minute rinses in sodium carbonate buffer.
Gently slide the glass slide housing the microspheres into the sodium carbonate buffer solution.
Cover the vial with aluminum foil.
Place the vial on a tilt tray set at 5 degrees and 5 rpm.
Gently remove the glass slide from the vial.
Slide the glass slide into another vial filled with DDI H2O covered with aluminum foil.
Place the vial on the tilt tray for 10 minutes at the same speed and tilt angle as before.
Repeat this step twice with fresh water each time.
Remove the glass slide from the vial after rinsing.
Dry the glass slide in an oven set at 80°C for 10 minutes before imaging.
Prepare a 10 μg/mL solution of Texas-Red avidin in phosphate buffered saline.
Add the solution to a 60 mL polypropylene vial with a hinged cap.
Gently slide the glass slide containing a biotin-terminated microsphere into the solution, covering only the microsphere.
React for 30 minutes at room temperature in the dark.
Remove excess fluorophore through two 10 minute rinses of the microspheres in PBS buffer.
Fill a 60 mL polypropylene vial with a hinged cap with PBS buffer.
Gently slide the glass slide into the solution, covering only the microsphere and not the cardboard housing.
Cover the vial with aluminum foil.
Place the vial on a tilt tray set at 5 degrees and 5 rpm.
Gently remove the glass slide from the vial.
Slide the glass slide into another vial filled with DDI H2O covered with aluminum foil.
Place the vial on the tilt tray for 10 minutes at the same speed and tilt angle as before.
Repeat this step twice with fresh water each time.
Gently remove the glass slide from the vial after each rinse cycle.
Dry the glass slide in an oven set at 80 °C for 10 minutes before imaging.
Identify correctly functionalized microspheres through optical microscopy.
Ensure the surface is defect- and contaminant-free after functionalization.
Use fluorescence microscopy to probe the quality and uniformity of surface coverage.
Check for uniformly dense coverage of biotin molecules on the surface.
